Adult Northern plains killifish typically attain a maximum standard length of 10 cm [Li = 10 cm], a size that positions them among the larger-bodied representatives of the genus Fundulus. Field surveys across their Great Plains range indicate that individuals rarely exceed this upper bound, with growth trajectories slowing markedly after the onset of reproductive activity. The total length at which puberty is reached has been documented at 4.0 cm [Lp = 4.0 cm], a threshold that corresponds to the initial appearance of secondary sexual dimorphism in fin morphology and body depth. This life-history transition is reached relatively early compared to the ultimate length, suggesting a strategy that prioritizes early maturation in ephemeral and fluctuating prairie stream habitats. The magnitude of juvenile growth necessary to reach this pubertal size is substantial when one considers the exceedingly small mass at which exogenous feeding begins.

Neonatal wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.0046 grams [Wwb = 0.0046 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of 2.06 mm and the corresponding spherical volume calculation. This diminutive initial mass, characteristic of small-bodied cyprinodontiforms, imposes a narrow window of vulnerability during the yolk-sac larval stage when endogenous reserves must sustain the developing individual until the onset of exogenous feeding. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Fundulus heteroclitus reveal that the Northern plains killifish produces slightly smaller neonates, a pattern that may reflect adaptation to the thermal variability of interior continental stream systems rather than coastal salt marsh environments. The rapid depletion of yolk nutrients during the first days post-eclosion places a premium on the timely availability of suitable microcrustacean prey.

At the opposite end of the size spectrum, the ultimate wet weight attained by mature individuals reaches approximately 7.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 7.3 grams], a mass that results from an allometric relationship with the ultimate standard length. This moderately small adult body mass is consistent with the species' life in shallow, often intermittent prairie streams where energetic demands of foraging in warm, productive waters must be balanced against the constraints of elevated basal maintenance requirements. Field-captured adults sampled during the summer months frequently exhibit body condition indices that reflect the pulsed availability of aquatic invertebrates following seasonal rainfall events. The mass-length relationship underlying this asymptote has been derived from extensive morphometric data sets spanning multiple populations across the species' range, confirming the robustness of the 7.3 grams [Wwi = 7.3 grams] estimate as a population-level mean.

Lifespan data from mark-recapture studies conducted under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C] reveal that the time since birth at death averages 803 days [am = 803 days], equivalent to approximately 2.2 years. This comparatively short maximum longevity is typical of small-bodied annual or semi-annual killifish that exploit ephemeral aquatic habitats, where the risk of habitat desiccation imposes strong selective pressure for rapid completion of the life cycle. The influence of temperature on the rate of physiological aging is particularly pronounced in this species, as metabolic processes accelerate with increasing thermal regime, thereby compressing the window for reproductive output. Individuals maintained at cooler temperatures in ancillary experiments have demonstrated extended lifespans, highlighting the plasticity of the aging trajectory. The 23 °C [T = 23 °C] thermal regime under which these maximum longevity data were collected approximates the mean summer water temperature typical of the species' native range in the central Great Plains.

Reproductive output in Fundulus kansae is characterized by a modest fecundity schedule that reflects the constraints imposed by small body size. Gravid females collected during the spawning season were found to produce between 120 and 180 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 120 and 180 eggs per spawning event], with individual spawning events occurring at intervals of approximately 10 to 14 days across the breeding period. The combination of this clutch size with the observed frequency yields an estimated annual reproductive output of several hundred offspring per female, a figure that is consistent with the species' status as an iteroparous, fractional spawner adapted to the stochastic environmental conditions of prairie stream ecosystems. The relatively small egg diameter of 2.06 mm contributes to the low neonatal mass and influences the trade-off between offspring size and number that is central to the species' reproductive ecology. Continued monitoring of populations across latitudinal gradients is needed to assess the degree of plasticity in these reproductive parameters.
